sections.section_title: Introduction to Mudrā and the Significance of Hands
sections.content: This section introduces mudrā as a device to harness latent spiritual power, defining it as a mental attitude expressed through bodily postures and hand-poses. In tantric literature, the body is a temple and the hands are its gateways. The etymology of the Sanskrit word for hand, 'hasta', is given as 'that which blossoms out' ('hasati vikasati'). The Mahābhārata (Āśvamedhika-parva) is cited to emphasize the spiritual nature of hands, with Indra as their patron deity. A Sanskrit śloka from the epic is included. The hand is described as consisting of the palm (kara-tala) and five fingers (aṅguli), with 'pañca-śākhā' (five-forked) being a synonym for hand.
sections.summary: Introduces the concept of mudrā as a spiritual tool, highlighting the symbolic importance of the hands in tantric philosophy as gateways to the temple of the body, supported by etymology and scriptural references.

sections.section_title: The Symbolism of the Fingers and Ritual Placement (Nyāsa)
sections.content: This part details the significant Sanskrit names and symbolism of the five fingers. The thumb (aṅguṣṭha) is associated with the sacred waters of Brahmā. The forefinger (tarjjanī) is linked to rebuking or warning. The middle-finger (madhyamā) signifies consciousness as vibration. The ring-finger (anāmikā) is 'nameless' due to a mythological event involving Śiva and Brahmā. The little-finger (kaniṣṭhā) is the weakest. The section then explains the preliminary rituals of aṅga-nyāsa (placement of divinities on the body) and kara-nyāsa (placement on the hands). Kara-nyāsa involves the five fingers, the palm (kara-tala), and the back of the hand (kara-pṛṣṭha). Two alternative procedures are mentioned: one using only the five fingers, and another including the palm and back of the hand as a sixth unit (ṣaḍaṅga-pak-śa). Verses from Prapañca-sāra are quoted.
sections.summary: Explores the symbolic meaning behind each finger in Sanskrit tradition and introduces the ritual practices of aṅga-nyāsa and kara-nyāsa, where divine energies are ceremonially placed on the body and hands.

sections.section_title: Mudrās in Ritual Practice: Aṅga-nyāsa and Mānasa-pūjā
sections.content: This section describes the practical application of finger combinations in aṅga-nyāsa for touching different parts of the body (heart, head, tuft of hair, eyes) while reciting specific mantras. It then moves to mānasa-pūjā (mental worship), where the five fingers are used to symbolize the five services (pañcopacāra): offering unguents (gandha), flowers (puṣpa), incense (dhūpa), light (dīpa), and food (naivedya). Each service corresponds to a specific mudrā (gandha-mudrā, puṣpa-mudrā, etc.) formed by touching the thumb to different fingers. This ritual represents the five primary elements (pañca-bhūta): earth, space, air, fire, and water. The Vaiṣṇava interpretation is also provided, where the finger manipulations represent five forms of Viṣṇu.
sections.summary: Details the use of specific finger combinations for ritual placement on the body (aṅga-nyāsa) and for performing mental worship (mānasa-pūjā), where each finger symbolizes a different offering and corresponds to one of the five cosmic elements.

sections.section_title: The Principle, Classification, and Purpose of Mudrās
sections.content: The underlying principle of mudrās is explained as a method to crystallize attention and facilitate absorption, leading to total involvement in worship. A quote from Nandikeśvara on dance gestures is used to illustrate this principle. The text clarifies that a mudrā's meaning is context-dependent. Mudrās are classified based on their function: for sequences of worship (āvāhanādi-mudrā), deity-specific (devatā-mudrā, e.g., liṅga-mudrā), and for achieving specific results (e.g., jñāna-mudrā for knowledge, astra-mudrā for protection). Some mudrās resemble the form of the deity (e.g., Varāha) or their attributes (e.g., Kṛṣṇa's flute). A tantric rule, 'kāmanā-bhedena aṅguli-bhedaḥ' (manipulation of fingers follows the desires of the devotee), is introduced, explaining how different finger combinations are used for different purposes like pacification, black magic, or immobilization.
sections.summary: Explains that mudrās function by focusing the mind to achieve deep spiritual involvement. It classifies mudrās by their use in worship sequences, their association with specific deities, and their intended outcomes, from spiritual attainment to magical rites.

sections.section_title: Groups of Mudrās and Textual Sources
sections.content: This section discusses variations in practice between different tantric schools (dakṣiṇa-mārga vs. vāma-mārga) and introduces several groups of mudrās, such as pañcopacāra mudrās, pañca-mudrā of Bhairavi-tantra, nivedanādi-mudrās, the ten nyāsa-mudrās, ten śrī-vidyā-mudrās, and twenty-four gāyatri-mudrās. It focuses particularly on the ṣaṇ-mudrā, a group of six used in invocation sequences: āvāhanī, sthāpanī, saṁnidhāyinī, saṁrodhinī, sammukha, and prārthanī. Each of these is described in detail with accompanying Sanskrit verses. The commentary on Tantra-rāja-tantra is quoted to give deeper philosophical meanings to invocation (āvāhana), placement (saṁnidhāpana), restraint (saṁnirodhana), and veiling (avagunṭhana). The section also notes that while Āgama texts enumerate 108 mudrās, fewer are in common practice. Early texts like Tantra-rāja-tantra, Mṛgendrāgama, and Rauravāgama list smaller numbers (20, 14, and 9 respectively).
sections.summary: Surveys various groups of mudrās used in different tantric traditions and rituals, with a detailed focus on the six invocation mudrās (ṣaṇ-mudrā). It also provides a historical overview by referencing the number of mudrās described in different Agamic and Tantric texts.

sections.section_title: Mudrās in Specific Ritual Sequences and Connection to Dance
sections.content: This final section details the use of mudrās in specific worship sequences like kalasa-pūjā (consecrating water) and the pañca-pātra sequence (offering water from five vessels). A summary of a complete worship ritual is given, showing the flow from invocation using ṣaṇ-mudrā to dismissal (visarjana) with the mudrās in reverse. A significant connection is drawn between worship mudrās and the hand gestures (hastas) of classical Indian dance as codified by Bharata-muni in the Nāṭya-śāstra. The text notes that most worship mudrās are samyuta-hastas (using both hands). Bharata's four-fold classification of hand gestures is also mentioned as relevant. The chapter concludes by listing various actions and feelings that mudrās can suggest, such as pulling, pushing, joining, cutting, and protecting, emphasizing that mudrās differ according to their specific purpose (uddeśa).
sections.summary: Illustrates the application of mudrās in specific rituals like water consecration and outlines the structure of a full worship service. It connects the practice of mudrā to the classical dance gestures of Nāṭya-śāstra and concludes by explaining how different manipulations of the fingers convey a wide range of actions and intentions.

chapter_summary: Chapter Two, 'The Modes of Mudrās', provides a comprehensive exploration of the role and significance of hand gestures (mudrās) in Hindu spiritual and ritual traditions, particularly within the tantric framework. It begins by establishing the hand as a potent spiritual gateway, detailing the symbolic meanings of each finger. The chapter explains the practical application of mudrās in rituals like 'nyāsa' (divine placement) and 'mānasa-pūjā' (mental worship), linking them to the five cosmic elements and different forms of deities. It delves into the underlying principle of mudrās as tools for focusing the mind and achieving complete absorption in worship. The text classifies various mudrās based on their function, purpose, and association with specific deities or outcomes. It provides detailed descriptions of important groups of mudrās, such as the 'ṣaṇ-mudrā' used for invocation, and references several historical texts to show the evolution of their practice. The chapter concludes by drawing a strong parallel between ritual mudrās and the hand gestures of classical Indian dance, highlighting their shared origin and expressive power.
key_arguments: Mudrā is not merely a physical hand-pose but a 'mental attitude' that harnesses latent spiritual power, deeply integrated into tantric philosophy where the body is a temple.
The hands and fingers have profound, inherent symbolism, with each finger corresponding to specific deities, concepts, and cosmic elements.
The primary purpose of using mudrās in worship is to crystallize the practitioner's attention, facilitate deep absorption (samādhi), and ensure total involvement of the being.
Mudrās are context-dependent and are classified by their function in ritual sequences, their specificity to deities, or their intended results, ranging from spiritual liberation to worldly goals.
There is a direct lineage and shared semiotic foundation between the mudrās used in religious worship and the 'hastas' (hand gestures) codified in classical Indian dance (Nāṭya-śāstra).
key_takeaways: The hands are considered spiritually significant 'gateways' in tantric practice.
Each finger has a specific name and symbolic association in Sanskrit tradition.
Rituals like 'kara-nyāsa' and 'mānasa-pūjā' use a precise language of finger-gestures to interact with the divine.
The use of mudrās is a technique for mental and spiritual focus.
There are numerous categories and groups of mudrās, with the 'ṣaṇ-mudrā' for invocation being one of the most important.
The practice of mudrā is documented in various ancient texts, including the Āgamas and Tantras.
The art of mudrā in worship is closely related to the expressive hand gestures of Indian classical dance.

historical_figures.name: Indra
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in the Mahābhārata as the divine overseer of the hands, highlighting their spiritual importance.

historical_figures.name: Brahmā
historical_figures.significance: The sacred waters of Brahmā are said to reside at the base of the thumb. A myth involving Śiva cutting off one of his heads is used to explain the name of the ring-finger ('anāmikā').

historical_figures.name: Śiva
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a myth where he cuts off one of Brahmā's heads with his ring-finger, rendering the finger 'nameless' ('anāmikā'). The 'liṅga-mudrā' is specific to his worship.

historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu
historical_figures.significance: In Vaiṣṇava worship, the five finger-manipulations in mānasa-pūjā represent his five forms: Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. The 'śaṁkha-mudrā' is specific to his worship.

historical_figures.name: Nandikeśvara
historical_figures.significance: Quoted for his explanation of the purpose of hand-poses in dance, which is used to illustrate the principle of how mudrās focus attention and evoke emotion.

historical_figures.name: Bharata-muni
historical_figures.significance: His codification of hand gestures (hastas) in the Nāṭya-śāstra is cited as being directly relevant to the mudrās used in worship, particularly his division of 'samyuta-hastas' (two-handed gestures).
historical_figures.dates: Traditionally dated between 200 BCE and 200 CE

quotations.quote: हस्तावाध्यात्ममित्याहुरध्यात्मविदुषो जनाः । अधिभूतं च कर्माणि शक्रस्तत्राधिदैवतम्॥
quotations.context: Pointing out the occult or spiritual nature of the hands, with Indra as their patron-deity.

quotations.quote: अङ्‌गुलीषु क्रमादङ्‌गैरङ्गुष्ठादषुि विन्यसेत्। कनिष्ठान्तासु तद्वाह्यतलयोः कल्पयेत् सुधीः ॥ अथ करन्यासप्रकार उच्यते- उभाभ्यां कराभ्यां तत्तदङ्गुष्ठाद्यङ्गुलीषु क्रमेणाङ्‌गुलीमूलमारभ्य मन्त्रपूर्वकं अङ्‌गुष्ठाभ्यां नमः' इत्यादि न्यसेत्।।
quotations.context: Describing the process of kara-nyāsa (placement on the hands).

quotations.quote: अङ्गुष्ठानामिकाभ्यां तु वश्यकर्मणि तर्पयेत्। अङ्गुष्ठमध्यमाभ्यां तर्पयेच्छान्ति कर्मणि । तर्जन्यङ्गुष्ठयोगेन तर्पयेदभिचारिके। कनिष्ठाङ्‌गुष्ठयोगेन स्तम्भने तर्पयेत् प्रिये ॥
quotations.context: Explaining which finger combinations to use for different rites (securing a woman, pacification, black magic, arresting an enemy).

quotations.quote: yato hastas tato dṛṣṭiḥ... yato dṛṣṭis tato manaḥ... yato manas tato bhāvaḥ... yato bhāvas tato rasaḥ
quotations.context: Explaining the purpose of hand-poses in dance, used as an analogy for how mudrās focus the mind and crystallize emotion in worship.

quotations.quote: हस्तौ तु प्राञ्जली कृत्वाऽनामिकामूलपर्वणोः । अङ्गुष्ठौ निक्षिपेत्सेयं मुद्रा त्वावाहनी मता ॥
quotations.source: Unattributed, likely from a ritual manual.

quotations.quote: भो स्वामिन् जगतां नाथ यावत्पूजावसानकम्। तावत्संप्रीतिभावेन बिम्बेऽस्मिन् सन्निधौ भव ॥
quotations.source: Unattributed, likely from a Vaiṣṇava manual.
quotations.context: The prayer recited while assuming the prārthanā-mudrā in Vaiṣṇava worship.

quotations.quote: विश्वात्मिकाया ललितायाः आह्वानं नाम परिच्छिद्यावेक्षणमिति सम्प्रदायः ॥
quotations.context: Explaining that invocation (āvāhana) signifies facility for perception and transaction.

images_and_diagrams.description: A set of six illustrations of hand gestures under the collective title 'Prāṇāhuti Mudrā'. The individual mudrās are labeled: Prāna, Apāna-Mudrā, Vyāna-Mudrā, Udāna-Mudrā, Samāna-Mudrā, and Grāsa-Mudrā.
images_and_diagrams.significance: Illustrates the mudrās associated with the five vital energies (prāṇas) and the offering of food.

images_and_diagrams.description: A set of eight illustrations of hand and body gestures under the collective title 'Nyāsa Mudrā'. The individual gestures are labeled: Mukha (face), Karapuja (hand worship), Hrdaya (heart), Sira (head), Sikha (tuft of hair), Kavaca (armor), Netra (eyes), and Astra (weapon).
images_and_diagrams.significance: Illustrates the hand positions used during aṅga-nyāsa, the ritual placement of divine energies on different parts of the body.

images_and_diagrams.description: A set of seven illustrations of two-handed gestures. The individual mudrās are labeled: Āvāhana-Mudrā, Sthāpana-Mudrā, Sannidhāpana-Mudrā, Sannirodhana-Mudrā, Sammukhi-Mudrā, Avagunthana-Mudrā, and Namaskāra-Mudrā.
images_and_diagrams.significance: Illustrates the key mudrās used in the sequence of invoking and establishing a deity during worship, part of the 'ṣaṇ-mudrā' group.

alternative_viewpoints.description: One procedure involves placement only on the five fingers, while the other (ṣaḍaṅga-pak-śa) includes the palm and the back of the hand as a sixth unit.

The practitioner of the right wing (dakṣiṇa-mārga) worships with the right hand and makes offerings with the left, whereas the practitioner of the left wing (vāma-mārga) does the opposite. Kaula-tāntriks are free to use any hand.
A different set of mantras/requests ('suprasanno bhava', 'varado bhava') is used in a variant procedure for infusing life into an icon, compared to the standard ṣaṇ-mudrā sequence.

alternative_viewpoints.viewpoint: Varying numbers of mudrās in different texts.
alternative_viewpoints.description: While Āgama texts enumerate 108 mudrās, earlier texts provide much smaller lists: Tantra-rāja-tantra (20), Mṛgendrāgama (14), and Rauravāgama (9), suggesting an evolution or variation in practice.
